title: Colourful Subtrees

source.name: Original exercise; classic technique (small-to-large merging, also called DSU on tree)

statement:
A tree has `n` vertices numbered `1` to `n` with root `1`. Vertex `v` has colour `c[v]`. For **every** vertex `v`, output the number of **distinct colours** among the vertices of the subtree of `v` (including `v`).

**Input.** The first line holds `n`. The second line holds `c[1] ... c[n]`. The third line holds `p[2] ... p[n]`, where `p[v]` is the parent of `v` and `p[v] < v`. (When `n = 1` the third line is empty.)

**Output.** `n` lines: the answer for vertices `1` to `n`.
hints: Doing one DFS per vertex is O(n^2) on a path. You need to reuse the colour sets of the children.
Give every vertex a set of colours and merge the child sets into the parent. Merging naively can still cost O(n^2) on a path-like tree if you always copy into a fresh set.

Small-to-large: when merging two sets always insert the elements of the **smaller** one into the **larger** one and keep the larger as the result. Each element moves only when its set at least doubles, so it moves O(log n) times and the total is O(n log n) insertions. Because p[v] < v you can process v from n down to 1 with no recursion.
editorial: Let `S(v)` be the set of colours in the subtree of `v`; the answer is `|S(v)|`. `S(v)` is the union of `{c[v]}` and the `S(child)`, so a bottom-up sweep with set unions works, and the only question is the cost of the unions. **Small-to-large merging** unions two sets by inserting the elements of the **smaller** into the **larger** and keeping the larger object (in C++ `swap` of two containers is `O(1)`, in Python and Java swap the references). An element is moved only when it sits in the smaller set, after which its set is at least twice as large as before, so any element moves at most `log2 n` times. Total insertions: `O(n log n)`, total time `O(n log n)` expected with hash sets or `O(n log^2 n)` with ordered sets. Since `p[v] < v`, processing `v = n, n-1, ..., 1` guarantees that when `v` is reached all of its children (they have larger labels) have already been merged into `S(v)`, so `ans[v] = |S(v)|` can be read immediately and then `S(v)` is merged into its parent; this avoids recursion, which matters in Python and Java for a path of 30000 vertices. The same idea answers any 'aggregate over the subtree' question whose per-vertex state is a mergeable container (counts per colour, the most frequent colour, sorted lists). An Euler tour with offline distinct-count queries (a Fenwick tree and last occurrences) is an alternative in `O(n log n)`; the tests were generated with that second method and cross-checked against explicit subtree collection.

import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])

# par[v] < v: process v from n down to 1

solutions.python:
import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
col = [0] + [int(x) for x in data[1:1 + n]]
par = [0, 0] + [int(x) for x in data[1 + n:n + n]]       # par[v] < v, so children have larger labels
sets = [None] + [{col[v]} for v in range(1, n + 1)]
ans = [0] * (n + 1)
for v in range(n, 0, -1):                                # every child of v is already merged into sets[v]
    ans[v] = len(sets[v])
    if v > 1:
        p = par[v]
        a, b = sets[v], sets[p]
        if len(a) > len(b):                              # small to large: always pour the smaller set
            a, b = b, a
        b |= a
        sets[p] = b
        sets[v] = None
print("\n".join(map(str, ans[1:])))
